section_summary: This section completes a detailed comparison of the Progressive, Liberal, Social Democratic, and Communist parties’ postwar programs, then presents American and Soviet assessments of Japan’s political institutions, parties, and ruling elites. It includes a weekly report on Japanese party activity, recommendations for registering parties and excluding compromised candidates, a roster of officers of wartime political organizations, and an interview with Progressive Party leader Tsurumi Yusuke. The final pages begin a broad review of the occupation through November 20, 1945, covering deployment, demobilization, civil liberties, educational and constitutional reform, and the dissolution of the zaibatsu.

subfiles.title: Political Parties in Japan: Developments During Week Ending November 17, 1945—Comparative Platforms (continued)
subfiles.from: Office of the United States Political Adviser, Tokyo
subfiles.to: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.about: Compares the economic, financial, labor, agricultural, social, cultural, educational, and women’s-rights programs of Japan’s principal postwar parties.
subfiles.summary: The continuation contrasts Progressive, Liberal, Social Democratic, and Communist proposals for economic control, taxation, inflation, labor organization, land reform, welfare, education, and women’s equality. Liberals generally favor private enterprise and removal of wartime controls, Social Democrats advocate planning and selective nationalization, and Communists call for worker management, confiscation, and the destruction of feudal relations. The concluding sections show broad agreement on expanded social protection and women’s political rights, but substantial differences over ownership and state control.

subfiles.title: Request for Declassification of Despatch on Japanese Political Parties
subfiles.from: Wilson C. Flake, Department of State
subfiles.about: Requests declassification of the November 17, 1945 despatch on Japanese political-party developments.
subfiles.summary: Form DS-507 for a confidential Atcheson despatch on political developments in the week ending November 17, 1945, reclassified as unclassified.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2211: Transmitting Translation of Article on the Ruling Classes of Japan
subfiles.about: Transmits a translation of M. Sokolov’s Soviet article “The Ruling Classes of Japan.”
subfiles.summary: Moscow Embassy forwards a translation of the article on Japan's ruling classes, with copies to Tokyo and Chongqing.

subfiles.title: The Ruling Classes of Japan
subfiles.about: Presents a Soviet Marxist interpretation of Japan’s constitutional order, landed and industrial elites, parliamentary parties, and militarism.
subfiles.summary: Sokolov argues the Meiji Constitution copied Prussian reaction, protecting landlords, capitalists and militarists; parliamentary forms hid a fascisized militarist state driven by Mitsui and Mitsubishi.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 74: Report on Japanese Political Parties and Candidate Restrictions
subfiles.from: George Atcheson Jr., Acting United States Political Adviser
subfiles.about: Forwards recommendations on party registration and candidate prohibitions, a weekly political report, and a roster of wartime political officials.
subfiles.summary: Atcheson says reappearance of former Political Association elements in the Progressive Party and chauvinist-led new parties prompted his recommendations; sends a memorandum to the Supreme Commander.

subfiles.title: Memorandum to the Supreme Commander: Registration of Parties and Prohibitions Against Certain Candidates
subfiles.from: George Atcheson Jr., Office of the United States Political Adviser
subfiles.to: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.about: Recommends compulsory party registration, disclosure of officers and finances, dissolution of successor organizations, and exclusion of influential wartime-organization members from candidacy.
subfiles.summary: Memorandum proposes barring influential officers of prohibited organizations from candidacy rather than all Diet members, requiring parties to disclose purposes, membership and funding, and dissolving successors of wartime organizations.

subfiles.title: Political Development During the Week Ending November 24, 1945
subfiles.from: John K. Emmerson, Office of the United States Political Adviser
subfiles.to: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.about: Surveys party organization, rallies, election prospects, rightist cooperation, and the activities of the Progressive, Liberal, Social Democratic, and Communist parties.
subfiles.summary: The report expects the Progressive Party to remain the largest Diet group despite losses, while Liberals and Social Democrats make gains, but notes widespread popular apathy caused by shortages of food, shelter, and clothing. Its appendices describe a rightist anti-Communist front, summarize speeches at the Progressive Party’s first mass meeting, and report provincial organizing by the Liberals and Social Democrats. The Communist appendix discusses Tokuda and Shiga’s leadership, Nosaka’s expected return from Yan’an, the dispute over the emperor, denials of Soviet financing, and willingness to cooperate in a democratic popular front.

subfiles.title: List of Officers of the Imperial Rule Assistance Association and Successor Organizations
subfiles.from: Office of the United States Political Adviser
subfiles.to: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.about: Lists known officers of the Imperial Rule Assistance Association, Imperial Rule Assistance Political Society, and Greater Japan Political Association.
subfiles.summary: The roster identifies presidents, vice presidents, directors, bureau chiefs, committee chairmen, regional officials, advisers, and councilors of Japan’s principal wartime political organizations. It was supplied to support screening of parties and election candidates for influential connections with prohibited organizations.

subfiles.title: Request for Declassification of Despatch No. 74
subfiles.from: Wilson C. Flake, Department of State
subfiles.about: Requests declassification of Despatch No. 74 concerning party registration and restrictions on candidates.
subfiles.summary: Form DS-507 on Atcheson's November 24, 1945 Despatch No. 74, changed from secret to unclassified.

subfiles.title: Department Instruction No. 3 Commending Japanese Political Reporting
subfiles.to: Acting United States Political Adviser to the Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.about: Commends John K. Emmerson’s reports on Japanese political parties and orders the praise placed in his efficiency record.
subfiles.summary: Department Instruction No. 3 commends Emmerson's despatches of November 1945 as high-standard reporting showing study and initiative.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 72: Interview with Tsurumi Yusuke of the Japan Progressive Party
subfiles.from: George Atcheson Jr., Acting United States Political Adviser
subfiles.about: Transmits a joint Allied Headquarters interview with Progressive Party leader Tsurumi Yusuke.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 72 on Tsurumi Yusuke: Progressives back regulated private ownership and a British-style monarchy, face war-responsibility problems, and hope to be a stable center and win a majority.

subfiles.title: Report of Joint Interview with Tsurumi Yusuke
subfiles.from: Technician Fourth Grade Selznick, Counter Intelligence Corps
subfiles.to: Lieutenant Pontius, Research and Analysis Section
subfiles.about: Records Tsurumi’s answers concerning the Progressive Party’s organization, program, constitutional position, war responsibility, and electoral prospects.
subfiles.summary: Tsurumi explains the Shimpoto's formation from former Political Association Diet members, advocating controlled private economy and constitutional monarchy while admitting its wartime taint and Tojo associates.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 73: Review of Developments in Japan, August 26–November 20, 1945
subfiles.from: George Atcheson Jr., Acting United States Political Adviser
subfiles.about: Transmits Robert A. Fearey’s reference review of developments during the first months of the occupation.
subfiles.summary: Atcheson sends a factual review of developments August 26-November 20, 1945, with copies to MacArthur, Willoughby and Crist.

subfiles.title: The Occupation of Japan: Report Covering August 26–November 20, 1945
subfiles.from: Robert A. Fearey, Office of the United States Political Adviser
subfiles.about: Reviews the occupation’s deployment, Japanese governments, demobilization, civil-liberties measures, educational and constitutional reform, and early zaibatsu-dissolution policy.
subfiles.summary: The report recounts the Allied landings, establishment of MacArthur’s headquarters, nationwide deployment, rapid demobilization, and destruction of Japanese military capacity. It contrasts the Higashikuni and Shidehara governments, then reviews directives freeing the press, releasing political prisoners, abolishing repressive controls, and reforming education. It also traces competing governmental and Privy Seal studies of constitutional revision and proposed electoral changes, including women’s suffrage. The surviving pages conclude with Allied pressure for industrial decentralization and the initial dissolution plans of Yasuda, Mitsui, Mitsubishi, and other zaibatsu.
